methods.name: Book-to-market (classic value)
methods.definition: buy high book/price, avoid low. Fama-French HML.
methods.evidence: Fama-French 1992. Value drew down ~55% from 2007 to mid-2020 (Arnott et al. 2021). HML is weak in large caps; the premium is concentrated in small stocks.
methods.why: earnings yield already failed, and B/M is weaker than E/P in large caps over 2010+.
methods.archive_note: Untested (earnings yield, a cousin, Tried-FAIL h20 t 0.91)

methods.name: Intangible-adjusted value
methods.definition: add capitalised R&D and SG&A to book before computing B/M.
methods.evidence: Arnott et al. 2021 show it "outperforms the traditional measure by a wide margin", but that is in-sample and designed after the drawdown.
methods.why: post-hoc fix for a failing factor; tiny edge in large caps at best.

methods.name: Composite value (E/P, CF/P, S/P, B/M average rank)
methods.definition: average several valuation ranks to cut noise.
methods.evidence: composites are standard in practitioner value (QMJ/AQR style). Jensen-Kelly-Pedersen cluster value signals into one theme that replicates globally.
methods.why: composites raise IC modestly (maybe 1.3-1.5x of one ratio), still likely below 0.03.

methods.name: Quality minus junk (QMJ)
methods.definition: long profitable, growing, safe (low leverage, low vol) firms.
methods.evidence: Asness-Frazzini-Pedersen 2019: significant risk-adjusted returns in US and 24 countries. Works in large caps (it is partly a low-risk bet).
methods.why: best-replicating "defensive" theme, but one component already showed nothing; return is mostly risk reduction, not raw return.
methods.archive_note: Untested (gross profitability, one leg, Tried-FAIL h20 -0.001)

methods.name: Piotroski F-score
methods.definition: 9 binary accounting checks, buy high-score value stocks.
methods.evidence: Piotroski 2000: ~23%/yr spread, but within high-B/M small firms, with returns concentrated in small, illiquid, low-analyst-coverage stocks.
methods.why: original effect lives in small, neglected stocks the S&P 500 does not hold.

methods.name: Accruals
methods.definition: low accruals (earnings backed by cash) beat high accruals.
methods.evidence: Sloan 1996. Listed among the strongest decayers after publication in McLean-Pontiff style studies; widely reported as largely gone after ~2000 in US large caps.
methods.why: well-known decay, small in large caps.

methods.name: Operating profitability (RMW)
methods.definition: Fama-French 5-factor profitability (operating profit / book equity).
methods.evidence: Fama-French 2015. Replicates in Hou-Xue-Zhang.
methods.why: near-duplicate of the GP test that showed zero.

methods.name: Asset growth / investment (CMA)
methods.definition: firms growing total assets slowly beat fast growers.
methods.evidence: Cooper-Gulen-Schill 2008: ~20%/yr spread over 40 years, but much larger in small caps; replicates per Hou-Xue-Zhang.
methods.why: one of the few that replicates value-weighted; large-cap IC still likely ~0.01, below what the testbed sees at h20 (needs h60/h250).

methods.name: Net share issuance / buybacks
methods.definition: firms shrinking share count beat issuers.
methods.evidence: Pontiff-Woodgate 2008: more significant than size, B/M or momentum post-1970; international version. Buyback announcement drift: Ikenberry-Lakonishok-Vermaelen 1995 (12% 4-year abnormal return, mostly value buybacks).
methods.why: robust and works in large caps, cheap to compute (shares outstanding in XBRL), but slow (h250) so the testbed has few independent periods.

methods.name: Low volatility / betting against beta
methods.definition: low-beta or low-vol stocks give similar return with less risk.
methods.evidence: Frazzini-Pedersen 2014 (BAB alpha needs leverage on the long side). Blitz-van Vliet 2007 show low-vol large caps match return at lower risk. Novy-Marx notes BAB partly reflects equal-weighting and small stocks (BABAB).
methods.why: real risk reduction, but long-only unlevered it lowers return; for a 10-year accumulator that is a cost, not a gain.
methods.archive_note: Tried-other (low-vol scorer inside the 51-name regime blend; regime ~+50% vs b&h +76.6%)

methods.name: Idiosyncratic volatility
methods.definition: avoid high residual-vol stocks.
methods.evidence: Ang-Hodrick-Xing-Zhang 2009: -1.31%/month extreme-quintile spread in 23 markets. Concentrated in small, high-vol, short-constrained stocks.
methods.why: short-leg effect, mostly small caps; S&P 500 has few extreme names.

methods.name: MAX (lottery stocks)
methods.definition: stocks with a huge max daily return last month underperform.
methods.evidence: Bali-Cakici-Whitelaw 2011 (JFE). Short-side, small-cap heavy.
methods.why: same as T-11; overlaps 1-month reversal which failed.

methods.name: Residual (idiosyncratic) momentum
methods.definition: momentum on factor-model residuals, not raw returns; less crash risk.
methods.evidence: Blitz-Huij-Martens 2011: about double the risk-adjusted return of raw momentum, 1930-2009.
methods.why: the best-argued momentum variant, but raw momentum showed nothing on confirm and post-2009 momentum has been weak.

methods.name: Industry momentum
methods.definition: buy stocks in last 6-12 months' winning industries.
methods.evidence: Moskowitz-Grinblatt 1999: explains much of stock momentum.
methods.why: rotation already lost; ~11 sectors means tiny breadth.
methods.archive_note: Untested, but the testbed uses sector-excess returns, which removes exactly this signal by design. Rotation on the 51 names: Tried-other (lost to b&h)

methods.name: 52-week-high proximity
methods.definition: stocks near their 52-week high keep rising.
methods.evidence: George-Hwang 2004: 0.45%/month, no long-run reversal.
methods.why: momentum family; correlated with the failed 12-1 test but behaves differently in crashes. Cheap to test.

methods.name: Momentum with crash protection (dynamic momentum)
methods.definition: scale momentum down after market falls and in high vol.
methods.evidence: Daniel-Moskowitz 2016: roughly doubles alpha and Sharpe vs static momentum, 1927-2013.
methods.why: scaling a signal with ~zero confirm IC does not create IC; it is a long-short hedge-fund tool.

methods.name: Return seasonality (Heston-Sadka)
methods.definition: a stock's return in calendar month m predicts its return in month m of later years.
methods.evidence: Heston-Sadka 2008 (1963-2002, NYSE/AMEX), international replication up to 5 years.
methods.why: survives in large caps and is cheap; but monthly signal on 500 names needs decades for power (see T-43).

methods.name: Earnings announcement premium
methods.definition: stocks about to announce earnings earn more in the announcement window.
methods.evidence: Savor-Wilson 2016: 9.9% annualised abnormal return for scheduled announcers.
methods.why: risk premium (less prone to arbitrage), but per-event size is a few bp, so turnover cost dominates for a retail account.
methods.archive_note: Untested (8-K 2.02 event study Tried-FAIL, but that measured post-event drift, not pre/during)

methods.name: Analyst revisions / estimate momentum
methods.definition: buy stocks with rising consensus EPS forecasts.
methods.evidence: Chan-Jegadeesh-Lakonishok 1996: earnings momentum separate from price momentum. Strong practitioner use.
methods.why: one of the few signals that still works in large caps, but needs point-in-time history of estimates (I/B/E/S, paid). Yahoo only gives today's snapshot.

methods.name: Short interest
methods.definition: avoid heavily shorted stocks; low short interest plus high volume is good news.
methods.evidence: Boehmer-Huszar-Jordan 2010: low-SI heavily traded stocks earn significant positive abnormal returns; high-SI negative but transient.
methods.why: real information, partly in large caps, but needs history. FINRA's API (docs, catalog) is free, twice a month, ~8 business days lag.

methods.name: Dividend initiations and omissions
methods.definition: drift after a firm starts (up) or cuts (down) a dividend.
methods.evidence: Michaely-Thaler-Womack 1995 (JF), 1964-1988 sample. Few S&P 500 events per year.
methods.why: pre-2000 evidence, tiny event count in large caps, event-study family already failed.

methods.name: Spin-offs
methods.definition: spun-off firms and parents outperform for 1-3 years.
methods.evidence: Cusatis-Miles-Woolridge 1993 (JFE), 1965-1988; driven by later takeovers.
methods.why: old sample, ~5-15 S&P events/year, no power.

methods.name: Index additions and deletions
methods.definition: trade S&P 500 inclusion announcements.
methods.evidence: Greenwood-Sammon 2025: addition effect fell from 7.4% (1990s) to under 1%; deletions ~0.1% 2010-2020.
methods.why: effect is gone.

methods.name: Customer-supplier lead-lag (customer momentum)
methods.definition: buy suppliers after their big customers rise.
methods.evidence: Cohen-Frazzini 2008: 1.22%/month EW, 1.06% VW long-short.
methods.why: strong paper and value-weighted works; but within S&P 500 few linked pairs, and customer disclosure (10-K segment notes, >10% customers) needs parsing. Recent decay unclear.

methods.name: Peer / technology / shared-analyst links
methods.definition: returns of economically related peers (patent overlap, co-coverage) predict a stock.
methods.evidence: Lee-Sun-Wang-Zhang 2019 "Technological links and predictable returns" (JFE) and Ali-Hirshleifer 2020 "Shared analyst coverage" (JFE); effects are monthly, partly large-cap.
methods.why: data paid (patents ok via USPTO free, co-coverage needs I/B/E/S). Cross-ref: the AI archive may cover text-similarity peers.

methods.name: Composite multi-signal score (fundamental law)
methods.definition: average many weak, low-correlated signals into one rank. Fundamental law: IR ≈ IC × sqrt(breadth) (Grinold 1989).
methods.evidence: Jensen-Kelly-Pedersen: 13 themes, most enter the tangency portfolio. Arithmetic: 5 uncorrelated signals of IC 0.008 combine to ~0.018, still below the 0.03 the testbed sees; and the long-only, no-short version captures only part (transfer coefficient ~0.3-0.5).
methods.why: the honest way to use weak signals, but even if real the net gain long-only on S&P 500 is maybe 0.5-1%/yr before tax drag on turnover, and you cannot verify it here.
methods.archive_note: Tried-other (8-scorer regime blend and learned weights lost to b&h on 51 names)

methods.name: Long-term reversal (3-5 year losers)
methods.definition: De Bondt-Thaler contrarian.
methods.evidence: largely subsumed by value and concentrated in small caps (Hou-Xue-Zhang).
methods.why: duplicate of value, no large-cap edge.

methods.name: Overnight vs intraday momentum split
methods.definition: momentum profit sits overnight, reversal intraday; trade the component.
methods.evidence: Lou-Polk-Skouras 2019: 14 strategies earn entirely overnight or entirely intraday.
methods.why: needs open/close execution; signal decomposes known factors that already failed. Free from Yahoo open/close.

methods.name: Turn-of-the-month
methods.family: B. Market-level timing and calendar effects
methods.definition: hold equities from last trading day to day 3 of the month.
methods.evidence: McConnell-Xu 2008: 1926-2005, all of the equity premium came at turns of month; 31 of 35 countries.
methods.why: for a buy-and-hold ISA investor, being out the rest of the month loses more than it gains after spreads; useful only as "time the monthly contribution a few days before month end" (tiny, free).

methods.name: Pre-holiday effect
methods.family: B. Market-level timing and calendar effects
methods.definition: day before market holidays has high returns.
methods.evidence: Ariel 1990 (JF). Pre-2000 evidence, widely reported weaker since.
methods.why: ~9 days/year, nothing actionable for a holder.

methods.name: Pre-FOMC drift
methods.family: B. Market-level timing and calendar effects
methods.definition: equities rise in the 24 hours before scheduled Fed announcements.
methods.evidence: Lucca-Moench: 0.49% per pre-FOMC window, 1994-2011. Kurov-Wolfe-Gilbert: disappeared after 2015.
methods.why: textbook post-publication decay.

methods.name: Equity premium predictors (CAPE, dividend yield, term spread)
methods.family: B. Market-level timing and calendar effects
methods.definition: time stock/bond weight on valuation or macro.
methods.evidence: Welch-Goyal 2008: no predictor beat the historical mean out-of-sample; 2024 update: a third of newer ones fail in-sample, half the rest fail out-of-sample.
methods.why: best-documented failure in finance; use as a behavioural "do not do this".

methods.name: Sell in May / Halloween
methods.family: B. Market-level timing and calendar effects
methods.definition: hold Nov-Apr only.
methods.evidence: Bouman-Jacobsen 2002 (AER) found it in 36 of 37 markets; in-sample, weak in recent US data, and cash half the year loses the premium.
methods.why: gives up ~half the equity premium for a small Sharpe gain.

methods.name: Post-publication decay
methods.family: C. Meta-evidence (how much to believe any of it)
methods.definition: discount published effects before testing.
methods.evidence: McLean-Pontiff 2016: -26% out-of-sample, -58% post-publication; bigger decay for bigger in-sample effects.
methods.why: as a planning rule ("expect 40% of the paper's spread, less in large caps") it would have predicted most FAILs; free to adopt in specs.

methods.name: Replication meta-studies (HXZ vs JKP vs Chen-Zimmermann)
methods.family: C. Meta-evidence (how much to believe any of it)
methods.definition: use what replicates as a shortlist.
methods.evidence: Hou-Xue-Zhang (65% fail, value-weighted, microcaps controlled; survivors: value, momentum, investment, profitability). Jensen-Kelly-Pedersen 2023: most replicate across 93 countries. Chen-Zimmermann: publication-bias shrinkage only ~12%.
methods.why: the disagreement itself is the lesson: they replicate as long-short multi-decade portfolios across all stocks, not as 2020+ large-cap ICs.

methods.name: Open Source Asset Pricing data instead of building signals
methods.family: C. Meta-evidence (how much to believe any of it)
methods.definition: download 200+ pre-computed predictors and their monthly portfolio returns.
methods.evidence: Chen-Zimmermann 2022, site: 98% of clearly significant predictors reproduce; portfolios in several implementations (VW, EW, quintile/decile, price/size screens) back to 1926.
methods.why: lets you check "does signal X still work in big stocks, post-2000, value-weighted" in minutes before writing any code. Firm-level signals are keyed by CRSP PERMNO (ticker mapping is the snag; CRSP itself is paid), so use the portfolio returns for triage, not as live signals.

methods.name: JKP global factor returns
methods.family: C. Meta-evidence (how much to believe any of it)
methods.definition: free factor returns for 153 factors in 93 countries, incl. large-cap ("mega/large") cuts.
methods.evidence: Jensen-Kelly-Pedersen, jkpfactors.com.
methods.why: answers "is this effect alive in UK/EU/global large caps" with no build; firm-level data needs WRDS (paid).

methods.name: Ken French data library as a reference
methods.family: C. Meta-evidence (how much to believe any of it)
methods.definition: free FF factors, momentum, industry and international portfolios, size breakpoints.
methods.evidence: Data library.
methods.why: needed for residual momentum (T-13) and to sanity-check factor ETF claims (T-60); free and daily-updated.

methods.name: Trading costs reality check
methods.family: C. Meta-evidence (how much to believe any of it)
methods.definition: subtract realistic costs before believing any backtest.
methods.evidence: Novy-Marx-Velikov 2016: anomalies with monthly one-sided turnover under 50% mostly survive costs, few above; a buy/hold spread (hysteresis band) is the best simple mitigation.
methods.why: adding a hold band to any future signal strategy is cheap and directly protects money; UK also has 0.5% stamp duty on UK shares (not on ETFs).
methods.archive_note: Untested in signal tests (backtest engine charges costs?)

methods.name: Multiple-testing hurdle t > 3
methods.family: C. Meta-evidence (how much to believe any of it)
methods.definition: raise the PASS bar as the number of tested signals grows.
methods.evidence: Harvey-Liu-Zhu 2016: new factors need t > 3.0. Harvey-Liu "Backtesting" haircut Sharpe ratios.
methods.why: Oracle has run 10+ pre-registered tests; at t>2 one false PASS is expected by chance. A count-aware bar (or Bonferroni/BHY) is free and prevents the most expensive mistake (trusting a lucky PASS).

methods.name: "Most stocks lose" skewness fact
methods.family: C. Meta-evidence (how much to believe any of it)
methods.definition: stock picking is a bet against extreme skew.
methods.evidence: Bessembinder 2018: 4% of stocks created all net US wealth 1926-2016; most stocks lifetime-underperform T-bills.
methods.why: strong argument for the index plan and against concentrated stock portfolios; show it in the GUI as a guardrail.

methods.name: Active fund failure rates (SPIVA)
methods.family: C. Meta-evidence (how much to believe any of it)
methods.definition: base rate for "can anyone beat the index".
methods.evidence: SPIVA Europe: ~95% of GBP global equity funds underperformed over 10 years.
methods.why: directly supports keeping real money in the index; prevents switching to an active fund after a bad year.

methods.name: Power calculation per signal before testing
methods.definition: compute minimum detectable IC from history length and IC volatility, publish it with each pre-registration.
methods.evidence: t ≈ mean IC / (sd IC / sqrt(T)). With monthly IC sd ~0.08-0.10 and true IC 0.01, you need ~250-400 independent months for t = 2. 2020+ confirm has ~70 months. (gate-02 power note already did this for h20/h5.)
methods.why: tells you up front which tests are pointless; saves build time. Make it automatic.

methods.name: Bigger universe (Russell 1000/3000, mid-caps)
methods.definition: more names = more breadth, smaller detectable IC.
methods.evidence: SE of a cross-sectional IC scales ~1/sqrt(N); going 500 to 3000 names cuts noise ~2.4x, but small names add the microcap illusions Hou-Xue-Zhang warn about.
methods.why: helps see effects, but free point-in-time Russell membership does not exist; survivorship worse than now; and effects found in mid/small caps do not help an index investor.

methods.name: International testbed (FTSE 350, STOXX 600, Japan)
methods.definition: second independent sample to confirm US findings.
methods.evidence: JKP show factors work out-of-sample in 93 countries.
methods.why: doubles sample, but point-in-time membership and fundamentals are hard; use JKP factor returns (T-37) instead first.

methods.name: Longer history (pre-2010)
methods.definition: extend train back to 1990s or 1960s.
methods.evidence: the cross-sectional literature uses CRSP 1926/1963+. Power grows with sqrt(months).
methods.why: real power gain, but Yahoo pre-2010 member coverage is poor (2010 already 31% missing) and XBRL starts 2009-2011. Only feasible via OpenAP portfolio returns (T-36).

methods.name: Portfolio sorts alongside IC
methods.definition: report top-minus-bottom quintile returns (value-weighted) as well as rank IC.
methods.evidence: the standard test in Hou-Xue-Zhang and Chen-Zimmermann; IC can hide nonlinear or tail-only effects.
methods.why: makes results comparable to papers and shows if only one tail works; does not add power.

methods.name: Fama-MacBeth / pooled panel with several signals at once
methods.definition: regress returns on many characteristics together each month, average slopes.
methods.evidence: Fama-MacBeth 1973.
methods.why: tests marginal value of a signal given others and uses one model instead of N separate tests (less forking).

methods.name: Newey-West and clustered standard errors
methods.definition: correct t-stats for overlapping horizons and cross-name correlation.
methods.evidence: Newey-West 1987; Petersen 2009 (cluster by time and firm).
methods.why: done; only firm-level clustering (Petersen) is missing, and NW over daily cross-sectional ICs already covers the overlap.
methods.archive_note: Tried-other (already in the harness: `signal_test.window_result` uses Newey-West t over the daily ICs; observed power is 2x the NW standard error)

methods.name: Deflated Sharpe ratio
methods.definition: correct a backtest Sharpe for number of trials and fat tails.
methods.evidence: Bailey-Lopez de Prado 2014.
methods.why: the backtest engine compares strategies vs b&h; DSR stops a tuned overlay looking good by luck. Simple formula.

methods.name: Probability of backtest overfitting (CSCV)
methods.definition: split history into blocks, check how often the in-sample best config ranks below median out-of-sample.
methods.evidence: Bailey-Borwein-Lopez de Prado-Zhu 2015; R package `pbo`.
methods.why: right tool whenever a parameter is chosen (MA length, rebalance bands); one-rule pre-registration already avoids most of it.

methods.name: Combinatorial purged cross-validation
methods.definition: many train/test splits with purging and embargo so overlapping labels do not leak.
methods.evidence: Lopez de Prado, *Advances in Financial Machine Learning* (Wiley 2018), ch. 7 and 12.
methods.why: more useful for the AI/ML side; for single pre-registered rules a fixed train/confirm split is fine.

methods.name: Delisting returns and survivorship correction
methods.definition: include the final return of delisted names (often -30% for performance delists).
methods.evidence: Shumway 1997: ignoring delisting returns biases anomaly results.
methods.why: missing losers bias early-period ICs toward quality/value and overstate b&h of single stocks; fixing it is hard with free data (SEC 25-NSE + last Yahoo price is a partial patch).
methods.archive_note: Untested (delisted names mostly missing in research.db)

methods.name: Forward paper tracking (already frozen)
methods.definition: freeze signals, judge on future data only.
methods.evidence: the only test immune to forking paths. McLean-Pontiff out-of-sample logic.
methods.why: honest, but 12 months of h20 is ~12 independent points; it will almost certainly be inconclusive. Pre-state that, and extend to 3 years.

methods.name: Benchmark hygiene (total return, same currency, same fees)
methods.definition: compare every strategy to total-return, GBP, after-cost index.
methods.evidence: price-only S&P 500 understates b&h by ~1.5-2%/yr (dividend yield). Boring-plan decision 1.
methods.why: removes a systematic bias that made earlier comparisons wrong-sized; certain gain in decision quality.

methods.name: Lowest-cost all-world fund
methods.family: E. Portfolio construction for the real money
methods.definition: pick the cheapest broad global tracker (accumulating, GBP).
methods.evidence: cost is the most reliable predictor of fund returns (SPIVA, T-42). Every 0.1% TER compounds to ~1% of the pot per 10 years.
methods.why: certain, measurable, permanent.

methods.name: Platform fee structure (flat vs percentage)
methods.family: E. Portfolio construction for the real money
methods.definition: move to a flat-fee platform once the pot is large enough.
methods.evidence: arithmetic (0.25-0.45% vs a few £/month).
methods.why: often the biggest single cost for a UK ISA, certain saving.

methods.name: Global vs home bias (all-world vs S&P 500 vs UK)
methods.family: E. Portfolio construction for the real money
methods.definition: hold world market weights, not US-only or UK-heavy.
methods.evidence: Anarkulova-Cederburg-O'Doherty: bootstrapped 39 developed countries 1890-2019; optimal lifetime mix ~33% domestic, 67% international stocks, beats age-based stock-bond. US-only looks best in hindsight (2010-2024), which is the trap.
methods.why: no expected-return gain is guaranteed, but it removes single-country risk at near-zero cost.

methods.name: 100% equities for a 10+ year horizon (no glide path yet)
methods.family: E. Portfolio construction for the real money
methods.definition: skip bonds while accumulating; consider de-risking only near the spend date.
methods.evidence: Anarkulova-Cederburg-O'Doherty: all-equity diversified internationally beats target-date style glide paths on wealth, retirement income and capital preservation.
methods.why: likely more terminal wealth; but tolerance of a -50% drawdown is the real constraint, and the paper is contested (US-centric critics).

methods.name: Factor ETFs (UCITS: value, momentum, quality, min vol, small-cap value)
methods.family: E. Portfolio construction for the real money
methods.definition: tilt part of the ISA to factor funds (e.g. iShares Edge MSCI World Value/Quality/Momentum/Min Vol, SPDR/Avantis small-cap value UCITS).
methods.evidence: factors replicate long-run (JKP) but decay post-publication (McLean-Pontiff), long-only funds capture maybe half, TERs 0.2-0.4%, and value lost for 13 years (Arnott et al.).
methods.why: small expected gain, high tracking error that tempts quitting at the worst time. Small-cap value is the most-cited tilt but UCITS options are limited.

methods.name: Multi-factor fund vs single factors
methods.family: E. Portfolio construction for the real money
methods.definition: one diversified multi-factor ETF instead of several single-factor tilts.
methods.evidence: combining low-correlated premia raises Sharpe (fundamental law, T-26); less timing temptation.
methods.why: better than single factors, still uncertain net of TER.

methods.name: Trend overlay (10-month MA)
methods.family: E. Portfolio construction for the real money
methods.definition: hold the index above its 10-month MA, cash below.
methods.evidence: Faber 2007/2013: equity-like return, bond-like drawdown since 1900. Zakamulin: data-mining contamination; no statistical outperformance post-1932, wins only in bear markets. Hurst-Ooi-Pedersen evidence is for diversified long-short futures, not one-index on/off. Harvey et al. show deterioration in 2009-2019 from more trend reversals.
methods.why: it will probably cut 2008's drawdown (PASS on drawdown is plausible) but 2020 and 2022 whipsaws make the <=1 pt/yr return cost the likely failure. Inside an ISA there is no tax cost, which helps.
methods.result: FAIL (research.db 2026-10-03): confirm 2008+ CAGR 8.1%, worst fall -26%; the overlay's own return-cost bar

methods.name: Time-series momentum across asset classes
methods.family: E. Portfolio construction for the real money
methods.definition: 12-month trend on equities, bonds, commodities, FX, long-short.
methods.evidence: Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen 2012; Hurst-Ooi-Pedersen since 1880.
methods.why: needs futures/leverage; UCITS managed-futures funds charge 1%+; weak 2011-2019.

methods.name: Dual momentum (Antonacci GEM)
methods.family: E. Portfolio construction for the real money
methods.definition: hold US or ex-US equities (whichever is stronger), switch to bonds if both lag T-bills.
methods.evidence: Antonacci backtests from 1974; post-publication (2014+) critiques (CXO) find it behind 60/40-like benchmarks.
methods.why: same family as T-62 plus a regional switch; post-publication record weak.

methods.name: Volatility targeting / vol-managed portfolios
methods.family: E. Portfolio construction for the real money
methods.definition: scale equity exposure inversely to recent volatility.
methods.evidence: Moreira-Muir 2017: large alphas. Cederburg et al. 2020: across 103 strategies, implementable versions do not beat unmanaged portfolios out-of-sample.
methods.why: without leverage it means less equity on average, i.e. lower long-run wealth; out-of-sample evidence negative.

methods.name: Risk parity
methods.family: E. Portfolio construction for the real money
methods.definition: weight asset classes by inverse risk, lever up bonds.
methods.evidence: depends on leverage and the 1982-2020 bond bull; 2022 stock-bond crash hit it hard.
methods.why: needs leverage, no fit for a long-horizon ISA accumulator.

methods.name: Bonds/gilts and glide path near spend date
methods.family: E. Portfolio construction for the real money
methods.definition: add gilts or a global bond fund only as the spend date nears.
methods.evidence: see T-59 (Anarkulova et al. against bonds for long horizons); conventional advice (target-date) for sequence risk.
methods.why: irrelevant for the first ~7 years, important in the last 3-5 before spending. Plan a review date, not a build now.

methods.name: Rebalancing rules
methods.family: E. Portfolio construction for the real money
methods.definition: annual or 5% bands.
methods.evidence: Vanguard 2010: no optimal frequency; annual or 5% bands balance risk and cost. Vanguard 2022 rational rebalancing: annual is optimal for most.
methods.why: with one all-world fund there is nothing to rebalance; a "rebalancing bonus" is not a reliable return source. Directing new contributions to the underweight fund is the free version.

methods.name: Lump sum vs drip-feed
methods.family: E. Portfolio construction for the real money
methods.definition: invest available cash at once rather than over 12 months.
methods.evidence: Vanguard UK: lump sum won 61.6-73.7% of rolling 1-year periods 1976-2022, ~1.2-2.4 pt average advantage.
methods.why: for windfalls, lump sum has higher expected value; monthly salary contributions are not DCA (invest each when received).

methods.name: Cash drag and contribution timing
methods.family: E. Portfolio construction for the real money
methods.definition: invest contributions the day they land; avoid idle cash in the ISA.
methods.evidence: at ~7%/yr expected equity return, a 2-week average delay costs ~0.25% of each contribution's first-year return (arithmetic). Turn-of-month (T-29) slightly favours buying just before month end.
methods.why: small, certain, free to fix with an automatic monthly investment.

methods.name: Stocks and Shares ISA first
methods.family: F. UK wrappers, tax and behaviour
methods.definition: £20k/yr allowance, no tax on gains or dividends.
methods.evidence: gov.uk ISAs.
methods.why: certain tax saving vs a GIA once over the small CGT/dividend allowances.

methods.name: SIPP / workplace pension with tax relief and employer match
methods.family: F. UK wrappers, tax and behaviour
methods.definition: put retirement money in a pension first: 20% relief added (25% uplift), 40/45% for higher-rate; employer match is free money; 25% tax-free at withdrawal.
methods.evidence: gov.uk pension tax relief.
methods.why: for money not needed before 57 (minimum pension age from 2028), relief plus match beats any return idea here. Add an "ISA vs pension" comparator.

methods.name: Lifetime ISA
methods.family: F. UK wrappers, tax and behaviour
methods.definition: up to £4k/yr, 25% government bonus, under 40 to open; penalty 25% if withdrawn except first home or age 60.
methods.evidence: gov.uk Lifetime ISA; Which? on the 25% charge.
methods.why: certain 25% uplift; the withdrawal penalty loses ~6.25% of own money if misused.

methods.name: Behavioural guardrails (automate, no-sell rules, loss pre-commitment)
methods.family: F. UK wrappers, tax and behaviour
methods.definition: automated monthly buy, written rule "no selling on drawdowns", show historical drawdowns before they happen, cool-off before any change to real allocation.
methods.evidence: the return gap between fund returns and investor returns is driven by timing flows (Morningstar "Mind the Gap" annual studies, ~1%/yr); Welch-Goyal shows timing does not work.
methods.why: avoiding one panic sale in a -30% year is worth more than any signal tested so far.

methods.name: Keep stock-picking money out of the ISA plan (or capped)
methods.family: F. UK wrappers, tax and behaviour
methods.definition: if signal trading ever goes live, cap it (e.g. 5%) in a separate pot judged against the all-world line.
methods.evidence: T-41, T-42 base rates.
methods.why: limits damage of a false PASS and keeps the experiment honest.

methods.name: FX and fund domicile (GBP-accumulating Irish UCITS)
methods.family: F. UK wrappers, tax and behaviour
methods.definition: prefer Irish-domiciled accumulating UCITS: 15% US dividend withholding (treaty) inside the fund, no FX fee per trade, no dividend reinvestment drag.
methods.evidence: US-UK treaty rate 15% vs 30% default; US ETFs are not available to UK retail (PRIIPs KID rule).
methods.why: avoids ~0.1-0.3%/yr of leakage vs badly chosen wrappers/share classes.

methods.name: Tax-loss harvesting
methods.definition: realise losses to offset gains.
methods.evidence: standard; irrelevant inside ISA/SIPP.
methods.why: no tax inside wrappers; only matters for a GIA beyond £20k/yr.

methods.name: Equal-weight S&P 500
methods.definition: equal-weight instead of cap-weight.
methods.evidence: historically higher return via size and rebalancing tilts; lagged badly 2023-2024 on mega-cap concentration. Higher TER and turnover.
methods.why: a size/value tilt in disguise, US-only, more tracking error.

methods.name: Pairs trading / statistical arbitrage
methods.definition: trade mean reversion between cointegrated pairs.
methods.evidence: Gatev-Goetzmann-Rouwenhorst 2006 (RFS) excess returns declined sharply after the 1990s; needs shorting and low costs.
methods.why: short-side, cost-sensitive, decayed; not doable in an ISA.

methods.name: Options overlays (covered calls, protective puts)
methods.definition: sell calls for income or buy puts for protection.
methods.evidence: buy-write indices (e.g. CBOE BXM) lag the index in bull markets; puts carry a premium cost. Options are not ISA-eligible in most UK platforms.
methods.why: lowers expected return or is not allowed in the wrapper.

methods.name: LLM headline sentiment (Lopez-Lira & Tang)
methods.definition: Ask an LLM "good/bad/unknown for the stock?" per headline, trade next-day on the score.
methods.evidence: GPT scores predict next-day returns; on post-cutoff headlines GPT-4 hits ~90% portfolio-day accuracy on the non-tradable day-0 reaction, the tradable drift is concentrated in small stocks and negative news, and strategy returns fall as LLM adoption rises; small models (GPT-1/2, BERT) fail (Lopez-Lira & Tang, arXiv 2304.07619 v6, 2025).
methods.why: Finishing the 32B run is cheap and is the only honest post-cutoff test, but the paper's own tradable drift sits in small caps and is decaying, and the post-cutoff window is too short for power at large caps.
methods.archive_note: Tried-FAIL (Laya small classifier, all runs). 32B local reader on ~64k post-cutoff headlines pending (job 732 cancelled at 13.8k/154.8k, resumable)

methods.name: Anonymised headlines (Glasserman & Lin distraction effect)
methods.definition: Replace company names with "Company X" before scoring.
methods.evidence: Anonymised headlines beat originals in-sample with GPT-3.5, strongest for large firms (the model's general knowledge distracts it); out-of-sample the difference loses significance (Glasserman & Lin, arXiv 2309.17322). Masking does not stop recall of dates/entities (Lopez-Lira, Tang & Zhu, arXiv 2504.14765).
methods.why: A one-flag A/B on the 32B reader; worth it only as a cheap arm, since post-cutoff the effect is not significant and it does not fix leakage.

methods.name: LLM embeddings plus a supervised return model (Chen, Kelly & Xiu)
methods.definition: Embed each article with an LLM, train a ridge/logistic model from embeddings to next-day returns.
methods.evidence: LLM embeddings beat technical signals and bag-of-words, especially for negation/complex articles, across 16 markets and 13 languages; fresh-news alerts give higher Sharpe; slow price response consistent with limits to arbitrage (Chen, Kelly & Xiu, SSRN 4416687).
methods.why: Better than prompting because it learns the mapping, but needs a long labelled text history; with a modern embedder that history is pre-cutoff (leaky). Viable only paired with A-24 (chronological models) or EDGAR text.

methods.name: SESTM supervised word model (Ke, Kelly & Xiu)
methods.definition: Screen words that co-move with returns, fit a two-topic model, score articles. No pretrained model, so no look-ahead from training data.
methods.evidence: On Dow Jones Newswires, strong daily long-short performance net of costs; most of the effect within 1-2 days of news and stronger in smaller stocks (Ke, Kelly & Xiu, NBER w26186).
methods.why: The one news model that can use the full 2010-2019 train window legally. Headline-only, free-source text is much thinner than newswires, and the signal is day-0/1 (hard at daily-close execution).

methods.name: FinBERT sentiment
methods.definition: Finance-tuned BERT classifier for sentence tone.
methods.evidence: Beats Loughran-McDonald and classic ML on labelled analyst sentences, biggest gain with small training sets (Huang, Wang & Yang, CAR 2023 / arXiv 2006.08097; model yiyanghkust/finbert-tone).
methods.why: Better tone labels, not better returns; Lopez-Lira finds BERT-size models do not forecast returns. Pretrained on pre-2020 text, so leakage is limited (a small plus).
methods.archive_note: Untested (Laya, a similar small classifier, FAILED)

methods.name: Loughran-McDonald dictionary tone baseline
methods.definition: Count negative/uncertainty words from the finance dictionary.
methods.evidence: Finance-specific lists beat general ones on 10-K tone vs filing returns (Loughran & McDonald, JF 2011).
methods.why: Useful only as the zero-leakage baseline every LLM text test should beat; weak on its own.

methods.name: LLM financial statement analysis (Kim, Muhn & Nikolaev)
methods.definition: Give an LLM anonymised statements, ask for next-year earnings direction.
methods.evidence: Claimed GPT-4 beats analysts (arXiv 2407.17866); the paper is now **withdrawn** after a co-author found replication inconsistencies (Nikolaev's notice).
methods.why: Withdrawn result, plus recall of pre-cutoff numbers makes backtests meaningless.

methods.name: Lazy Prices: 10-K/10-Q change detection
methods.definition: Cosine similarity between this filing and last year's; firms that change their text a lot underperform.
methods.evidence: Short "changers", long "non-changers": up to 188 bp/month alpha, predicts earnings, news and bankruptcies; investors are slow to notice (Cohen, Malloy & Nguyen, JF 2020). Headline number is the strongest spec; value-weighted and post-publication returns are smaller (decay: see quant archive).
methods.why: Best text candidate on paper: no LLM so no cutoff rule, full 2010+ testbed usable, slow quarterly signal (low turnover). Likely weaker in S&P 500 and since 2018 publication.

methods.name: Risk-factor (Item 1A) change detection
methods.definition: Diff only the risk-factor section; flag new or expanded risks.
methods.evidence: Lazy Prices finds risk-factor changes carry much of the effect (JF 2020); LLM pipelines can map 10-K risks into a taxonomy for S&P 500 (arXiv 2601.15247).
methods.why: Sub-variant of A-08; best value is as a user-facing "new risks this year" digest (see A-93).

methods.name: LLM semantic change in disclosures ("metric shifting")
methods.definition: LLM extracts emphasised metrics per period; firms that shift what they emphasise underperform.
methods.evidence: LLM-measured semantic shifts in disclosures predict alpha (arXiv 2510.03195).
methods.why: New, single paper; LLM-based so only post-cutoff filings count (one or two 10-K cycles).

methods.name: 8-K free-text classification beyond item codes
methods.definition: LLM reads 8-K bodies/exhibits to type events finer than item numbers.
methods.evidence: Item-code event studies already FAILED here (2.02, 1.01, 2.01, clusters).
methods.why: Finer types split already-weak events into smaller, lower-power buckets.

methods.name: Guidance extraction from 8-K Ex. 99.1
methods.definition: Pull management guidance numbers from press releases into a table.
methods.evidence: No free consensus to compute "guidance surprise"; useful as structured data (no return paper tested here).
methods.why: Good input for explanations (A-91) and for ML targets later; as a stand-alone signal it lacks the consensus benchmark.

methods.name: LLM-extracted supplier/customer edges (customer momentum)
methods.definition: Extract "major customer" links from 10-Ks; trade suppliers after customer news.
methods.evidence: Customers average 20% of supplier sales and customer returns predict supplier returns (Cohen & Frazzini, JF 2008); still present with updated methods (Customer Momentum, arXiv 2301.11394).
methods.why: Edges are a useful asset already half-built; the lead-lag is classic and testable on the full testbed if edges are dated, but suppliers in the S&P 500 are big and well covered.
methods.archive_note: Tried-other (relationship graph exists; no signal test)

methods.name: Capex/investment plans from calls (ChatGPT and corporate policies)
methods.definition: LLM reads calls for capex intentions.
methods.evidence: LLM-measured capex plans predict future firm investment (Jha, Qian, Weber & Yang, NBER w32161).
methods.why: Predicts investment, not returns directly; maps onto the investment anomaly (quant archive) that can be computed from XBRL instead.

methods.name: Earnings-call tone
methods.definition: Score management tone in prepared remarks vs Q&A.
methods.evidence: FinBERT shows call text more informative than dictionaries suggest (Huang et al.).
methods.why: Data access is the blocker; effect mostly priced at the call.

methods.name: Q&A evasiveness (non-answers)
methods.definition: Detect "we don't disclose / take it offline" replies.
methods.evidence: ~11% of analyst questions get non-answers, more when news is bad (Gow, Larcker & Zakolyukina, JAR).
methods.why: Interesting governance flag for a holding report, weak trading evidence.

methods.name: Earnings-call audio (vocal cues)
methods.definition: Emotion analysis of CEO/CFO voice.
methods.evidence: Vocal affect carries information beyond words (Mayew & Venkatachalam, JF 2012).
methods.why: Data and tooling cost far above any plausible large-cap edge.

methods.name: Stale vs novel news
methods.definition: Down-weight repeated stories; novelty filter before scoring.
methods.evidence: Investors overreact to stale news, which reverses (Tetlock, RFS 2011).
methods.why: A sensible preprocessing step for A-01/A-03 (dedupe), not a signal by itself here.

methods.name: Event typing taxonomy for news
methods.definition: Classify articles into typed events (M&A, guidance cut, lawsuit) then study each.
methods.evidence: Laya already typed relevance/direction per article and FAILED.
methods.why: Already tried; more categories cut power further.

methods.name: Aggregate news sentiment for market timing
methods.definition: Daily market-wide LLM mood to tilt equity exposure.
methods.evidence: 4B regime tilt here moved weights on 24% of days and added noise.
methods.why: Already failed; market timing has the lowest power of all (one series).

methods.name: International / multilingual news
methods.definition: Extend A-01/A-03 to non-US stocks in local languages.
methods.evidence: Predictability across 16 markets, 13 languages (Chen, Kelly & Xiu).
methods.why: Less efficient markets help, but no international testbed yet (ticket 08 needs-triage) and ISA costs on foreign single stocks are high.

methods.name: LLM forecast of earnings or prices directly
methods.definition: Ask a model "what will EPS/price be?"
methods.evidence: LLMs recall exact pre-cutoff economic and market values; instructions not to use them fail (Lopez-Lira, Tang & Zhu, arXiv 2504.14765).
methods.why: Below base rate already; backtests impossible pre-cutoff.

methods.name: Memorisation probe for the local models' real cutoff
methods.family: 2. LLM agents, benchmarks and point-in-time models
methods.definition: Before trusting "cutoff 2025-05-31", test whether qwen recalls prices, headlines or EPS after that date; set the cutoff empirically.
methods.evidence: LLMs recall exact pre-cutoff values and masking fails (arXiv 2504.14765); best agents lose up to 50% and fall to zero after their knowledge window (Profit Mirage, arXiv 2510.07920).
methods.why: Cheap insurance that the one rule protecting every LLM verdict is right; protects decisions, not returns.
methods.archive_note: Untested (cutoff rule exists, declared not measured)

methods.name: Chronologically consistent LLMs (ChronoBERT / ChronoGPT)
methods.family: 2. LLM agents, benchmarks and point-in-time models
methods.definition: Use models trained only on text up to each year (vintages 1999-2024) so pre-2025 history can be tested without look-ahead.
methods.evidence: Yearly vintages, ~1.55B params, match BERT on NLP and get Sharpe close to a much larger Llama on next-day news returns, implying look-ahead bias is modest (He, Lv, Manela & Wu, arXiv 2502.21206; weights on Hugging Face, manelalab).
methods.why: The only way to give any LLM text signal the full 2010-2019 train / 2020+ confirm testbed, fixing the power problem; still needs a signal that works.

methods.name: Point-in-time commercial models (PiT-Inference) and Look-Ahead-Bench
methods.family: 2. LLM agents, benchmarks and point-in-time models
methods.definition: Vendor LLMs with dated cutoffs; benchmark measures alpha decay across regimes.
methods.evidence: Llama 3.1 and DeepSeek show clear look-ahead bias; PiT models generalise better (Benhenda, arXiv 2601.13770, code).
methods.why: A-24 gives the same benefit locally and free; single-author benchmark.

methods.name: TradingAgents (multi-agent debate desk)
methods.family: 2. LLM agents, benchmarks and point-in-time models
methods.definition: Analyst, bull/bear, risk and trader agents debate each trade.
methods.evidence: Reports better return/Sharpe than baselines on a short window of a few large-cap stocks (arXiv 2412.20138); such reported alpha suffers temporal contamination, missing frictions and short windows (Alpha Illusion, arXiv 2605.16895).
methods.why: Same family as the agent that already underperformed base rate; debate adds tokens, not information.

methods.name: FinMem / FinAgent / FinCon memory agents
methods.family: 2. LLM agents, benchmarks and point-in-time models
methods.definition: Agents with layered memory and reflection.
methods.evidence: Short single-stock backtests (FinMem, arXiv 2311.13743; FinAgent, arXiv 2402.18485); flagged as non-deployment evidence (arXiv 2605.16895).
methods.why: Look-ahead-prone, tiny samples, needs large models.

methods.name: StockBench-style evaluation
methods.family: 2. LLM agents, benchmarks and point-in-time models
methods.definition: Contamination-free multi-month daily trading test of agents.
methods.evidence: Mar-Jul 2025; most agents (GPT-5, Claude 4, Qwen3, etc.) fail to beat buy-and-hold (arXiv 2510.02209).
methods.why: Confirms the oracle's own finding; adopt its metrics, do not expect a different answer.

methods.name: FinBen and Q&A benchmarks
methods.family: 2. LLM agents, benchmarks and point-in-time models
methods.definition: 36-dataset benchmark incl. a trading task.
methods.evidence: Only >70B models handle trading; trading results on short windows (arXiv 2402.12659).
methods.why: Useful only to pick an extraction model; trading part is leak-prone.

methods.name: Reporting protocol for any LLM claim (Alpha Illusion P1-P6)
methods.family: 2. LLM agents, benchmarks and point-in-time models
methods.definition: Checklist: post-cutoff only, costs, window length, baseline, factor exposure, uncertainty.
methods.evidence: Alpha Illusion, arXiv 2605.16895; leakage benchmark FinLake-Bench.
methods.why: Mostly in place; add the factor-exposure check (does an "AI pick" just load on momentum/size?).
methods.archive_note: Tried-other (pre-registration and cutoff rule already cover most)

methods.name: LLM as an information interface, not a trader
methods.family: 2. LLM agents, benchmarks and point-in-time models
methods.definition: LLM extracts facts; separate calibrated statistical modules decide.
methods.evidence: Recommended architecture in arXiv 2605.16895.
methods.why: Right design direction; benefit depends on the extracted facts being predictive.

methods.name: Fine-tune a small LLM on returns (FinGPT-style LoRA)
methods.family: 2. LLM agents, benchmarks and point-in-time models
methods.definition: LoRA-tune a 4-8B model on headline to return labels.
methods.evidence: FinGPT, arXiv 2306.06031 reports mostly classification benchmarks, not clean OOS trading.
methods.why: Base model already saw the labels (leak); A-03 or A-24 get the same with less cost.

methods.name: Verdict calibration
methods.family: 2. LLM agents, benchmarks and point-in-time models
methods.definition: Map research-agent confidence to real hit rates; shrink overconfident calls.
methods.evidence: GPT overconfidence hurts (Glasserman & Lin); own data: 56% vs 59.5% base.
methods.why: Calibrating a signal below base rate gives "ignore it", which is already the answer.

methods.name: Gu-Kelly-Xiu ML benchmark (trees and neural nets)
methods.family: 3. Supervised ML on characteristics (the XGBoost question)
methods.definition: Predict monthly returns from ~94 characteristics + macro with trees/NNs.
methods.evidence: NNs/trees roughly double regression-based strategy performance, gains from interactions; dominant inputs are momentum, liquidity, volatility; predictability also in large liquid stocks (Gu, Kelly & Xiu, RFS 2020). Payoff falls 62% excluding microcaps, 68% excluding distressed firms, and worsens after costs (Avramov, Cheng & Metzker, MS 2023).
methods.why: With 30-60 in-house characteristics and a rank target it becomes a fair test on the full testbed (no cutoff issue); S&P 500 large-cap gain is the small remainder.
methods.archive_note: Tried-other (user skipped XGBoost on weak inputs)

methods.name: Build a characteristic library (input breadth)
methods.family: 3. Supervised ML on characteristics (the XGBoost question)
methods.definition: Compute ~50 standard signals (value, quality, investment, accruals, issuance, vol, beta, liquidity, momentum family) point-in-time from XBRL and prices.
methods.evidence: 200+ published predictors replicated with code and definitions (Chen & Zimmermann, Open Source Asset Pricing); stock-level files are keyed to CRSP permno (WRDS needed to map).
methods.why: The prerequisite that would change the XGBoost verdict; also reusable for risk and explanations.
methods.archive_note: Building (XBRL fundamentals live; a few signals done)

methods.name: Gradient boosting (LightGBM/XGBoost) with rank target
methods.family: 3. Supervised ML on characteristics (the XGBoost question)
methods.definition: GBM on the A-35 library, target = next-month cross-sectional rank.
methods.evidence: Boosted trees among best GKX models (RFS 2020); trees/GBM on S&P 500 stat-arb returns declined to near zero after ~2010 (Krauss, Do & Huck, EJOR 2017).
methods.why: Cheapest strong learner; honest expectation is IC around the detection limit in large caps.

methods.name: Linear shrinkage: ridge, lasso, elastic net
methods.family: 3. Supervised ML on characteristics (the XGBoost question)
methods.definition: Penalised regression over many characteristics.
methods.evidence: Elastic net/ridge are GKX's linear baselines, beaten by nonlinear models but robust (RFS 2020); lasso on short-horizon returns finds sparse, short-lived signals (Chinco, Clark-Joseph & Ye, JF 2019).
methods.why: Should be run first: if ridge on 50 signals fails confirm, GBM is unlikely to rescue it.

methods.name: PLS / PCR (supervised factor compression)
methods.family: 3. Supervised ML on characteristics (the XGBoost question)
methods.definition: Compress many predictors into a few return-relevant components.
methods.evidence: Included in GKX comparison, below trees/NNs (RFS 2020).
methods.why: Same input limit, usually not better than ridge.

methods.name: Random forest
methods.family: 3. Supervised ML on characteristics (the XGBoost question)
methods.definition: Bagged trees.
methods.evidence: Below boosted trees and NNs in GKX (RFS 2020); also decayed in Krauss et al. (EJOR 2017).
methods.why: Dominated by A-36; keep only as an ensemble member.

methods.name: SVM / kernel methods
methods.family: 3. Supervised ML on characteristics (the XGBoost question)
methods.definition: Support vector classification of up/down.
methods.evidence: No strong cross-sectional asset-pricing evidence beyond what GBM/NN cover (Random Fourier Features in A-46 are the kernel analogue).
methods.why: No reason to expect it to beat GBM; scales poorly.

methods.name: Plain feed-forward neural nets
methods.family: 3. Supervised ML on characteristics (the XGBoost question)
methods.definition: 1-5 layer MLP on characteristics.
methods.evidence: NN3 best in GKX; gains shrink with economic restrictions (Avramov et al.).
methods.why: Needs ensembles of seeds and more data than ~500 stocks provide; GBM is safer on small panels.

methods.name: Ensembles and forecast combination
methods.family: 3. Supervised ML on characteristics (the XGBoost question)
methods.definition: Average many simple forecasts or models.
methods.evidence: Combining forecasts gives consistent OOS gains for the equity premium (Rapach, Strauss & Zhou, RFS 2010).
methods.why: The most reliable way to squeeze weak signals; can combine the "could not see" signals (momentum, SUE, EY with IC > 0) into one test with more power.

methods.name: Learning to rank (pairwise/listwise loss)
methods.family: 3. Supervised ML on characteristics (the XGBoost question)
methods.definition: Train directly on ordering stocks (LambdaMART, ListNet).
methods.evidence: Roughly 3x Sharpe vs naive ranking on cross-sectional momentum (Poh, Lim, Zohren & Roberts, arXiv 2012.07149).
methods.why: Right loss for a ranking IC test; cannot add information the inputs lack, and the 3x is relative to a weak baseline.

methods.name: Target design: excess return, rank, risk-adjusted, triple barrier
methods.family: 3. Supervised ML on characteristics (the XGBoost question)
methods.definition: Choose what the model predicts: sector-neutral rank, vol-scaled return, or triple-barrier outcome.
methods.evidence: Triple-barrier labels and sample weighting (López de Prado, Advances in Financial ML, Wiley 2018); GKX use plain excess returns.
methods.why: Rank and sector-neutral targets cut noise for little cost; that is where "better targets" can help weak inputs.

methods.name: Meta-labelling
methods.family: 3. Supervised ML on characteristics (the XGBoost question)
methods.definition: Secondary model predicts whether a primary rule's signal will pay, used to size or skip.
methods.evidence: Framework from López de Prado 2018; evidence is practitioner backtests, little independent OOS.
methods.why: Needs a primary signal with real edge; the only live candidate is the trend overlay (quant stream), and filtering it risks overfitting.

methods.name: Virtue of complexity (Random Fourier Features)
methods.family: 3. Supervised ML on characteristics (the XGBoost question)
methods.definition: Thousands of random nonlinear features of a few predictors for market timing.
methods.evidence: Claimed complex models beat simple ones (Kelly, Malamud & Zhou, JF 2024 / NBER w30217); critique: with P >> T the forecast is just a similarity-weighted average of past returns, a momentum-like rule (Nagel, BFI WP 2025-104).
methods.why: Market timing, contested, and the trend overlay already covers what it secretly does.

methods.name: Cost-aware ML portfolios
methods.family: 3. Supervised ML on characteristics (the XGBoost question)
methods.definition: Learn weights with trading costs in the objective instead of predicting then trading.
methods.evidence: ML profits deteriorate with realistic costs due to turnover and extreme positions (Avramov et al.).
methods.why: Matters only once a gross signal exists.

methods.name: LSTM on daily returns
methods.family: 4. Deep models trained from scratch (sequence, image, graph)
methods.definition: Sequence model on past returns per stock, rank next-day.
methods.evidence: S&P 500 1992-2015: 0.46%/day before costs, Sharpe 5.8 pre-cost, with profits largely gone in the later years (Fischer & Krauss, EJOR 2018; working paper).
methods.why: Daily short-term reversal in disguise, arbitraged away, killed by costs; reversal_1m already failed.

methods.name: Temporal conv nets / transformers on price-volume
methods.family: 4. Deep models trained from scratch (sequence, image, graph)
methods.definition: TCN or transformer on OHLCV windows.
methods.evidence: Same input as A-48; TSFM studies on single stocks show tiny, sparse gains over random walk (arXiv 2606.27100).
methods.why: Architecture does not fix the absence of signal in past prices of large caps.

methods.name: Transformer SDF across assets (AI asset pricing models)
methods.family: 4. Deep models trained from scratch (sequence, image, graph)
methods.definition: Attention across stocks inside the pricing kernel.
methods.evidence: OOS Sharpe 4.57 vs 1.05-1.80 for traditional models, full CRSP universe (Kelly, Kuznetsov, Malamud & Xu, NBER w33351).
methods.why: Needs the full CRSP panel; Sharpe of that size comes from hard-to-trade names.

methods.name: CNN on chart images ((Re-)Imag(in)ing Price Trends)
methods.family: 4. Deep models trained from scratch (sequence, image, graph)
methods.definition: Turn 5/20/60-day OHLC charts into images, CNN predicts up/down.
methods.evidence: CNN chart signals beat momentum/reversal, transfer to other markets and time scales; strongest at short horizons and in smaller stocks (Jiang, Kelly & Xiu, JF 2023).
methods.why: Credible, no look-ahead, full testbed usable; but weekly horizon means turnover and the large-cap effect is weak. A fun, honest test, low payoff.

methods.name: Graph neural nets over the supplier/sector graph
methods.family: 4. Deep models trained from scratch (sequence, image, graph)
methods.definition: GNN propagates signals along relationship edges.
methods.evidence: Relational ranking with industry/wiki graphs improved stock ranking in short US samples (Feng et al., TOIS 2019, arXiv 1809.09441).
methods.why: Test the simple lead-lag (A-13) first; a GNN is a heavier way to find the same link effect.

methods.name: Deep SDF with GAN (Chen-Pelger-Zhu)
methods.family: 4. Deep models trained from scratch (sequence, image, graph)
methods.definition: Adversarial network estimates the pricing kernel from characteristics and macro states.
methods.evidence: High OOS Sharpe on the full US cross-section 1967-2016 (Chen, Pelger & Zhu, MS 2024, arXiv 1904.00745).
methods.why: Research-grade, data hungry, gains in the full (small-cap) universe.

methods.name: Conditional autoencoder factors
methods.family: 4. Deep models trained from scratch (sequence, image, graph)
methods.definition: Neural net maps characteristics to factor loadings.
methods.evidence: Lower pricing errors than IPCA/Fama-French on full CRSP (Gu, Kelly & Xiu, J. Econometrics 2021).
methods.why: A pricing (explaining) tool more than a stock picker for 500 names.

methods.name: Chronos / Chronos-Bolt zero-shot return forecasts
methods.definition: Pretrained forecaster on each stock's return series.
methods.evidence: On large global daily excess returns, off-the-shelf Chronos gets OOS R² -1.37% and ~51% direction; TimesFM R² -2.80%, below 50% (Rahimikia, Ni & Wang, arXiv 2511.18578); models: Chronos, Chronos-Bolt card.
methods.why: Independent evidence says worse than predicting zero. Skip for returns.

methods.name: TimesFM, Moirai, Lag-Llama
methods.definition: Other general TSFMs.
methods.evidence: On AAPL/AMZN/GOOG/JPM/META, gains over random walk are "small and sparse"; only 2 of 10 tasks significant (arXiv 2606.27100); TimesFM, Moirai, Lag-Llama.
methods.why: Same as A-55.

methods.name: Finance-pretrained TSFMs (FinText-TSFM)
methods.definition: TSFMs pretrained on financial returns.
methods.evidence: Finance-pretrained models give "substantial forecasting and economic gains" vs off-the-shelf (arXiv 2511.18578).
methods.why: The only TSFM claim worth a test; pretraining window overlaps the testbed, so only post-release days are clean.

methods.name: TSFMs for volatility instead of returns
methods.definition: Forecast realised volatility for risk display/sizing.
methods.evidence: Volatility is persistent and forecastable with simple models (A-60); TSFM edge over HAR not established in the sources above.
methods.why: If vol forecasts are wanted, HAR is cheaper and just as good.

methods.name: GARCH volatility forecasting
methods.definition: Conditional variance model per stock/index.
methods.evidence: Standard (Bollerslev, J. Econometrics 1986).
methods.why: Volatility is genuinely predictable, unlike returns; useful for risk alerts and position-size display, not alpha.

methods.name: HAR realised-volatility model
methods.definition: Regress volatility on daily, weekly, monthly past volatility.
methods.evidence: Simple, hard-to-beat vol forecaster (Corsi, J. Fin. Econometrics 2009).
methods.why: Cheapest reliable forecast in this whole list; feeds A-95 risk monitor and the trend overlay's vol scaling (quant archive).

methods.name: Hidden Markov / Markov-switching regimes
methods.definition: Latent bull/bear states from returns and vol.
methods.evidence: Foundation (Hamilton, Econometrica 1989); here, an LLM regime tilt added noise.
methods.why: States are only clear in hindsight; switching lags make it a slower trend filter, which the pre-registered trend overlay already tests.

methods.name: Kalman filters (dynamic betas, pairs hedge ratios)
methods.definition: Track time-varying betas or spreads.
methods.evidence: Standard state-space tool; no specific large-cap alpha evidence found.
methods.why: Good for showing "this holding's beta rose", minor for returns.

methods.name: Bayesian shrinkage of the cross-section
methods.definition: Shrink many factor premia towards zero with a prior.
methods.evidence: Strong shrinkage over principal components yields robust SDFs from many anomalies (Kozak, Nagel & Santosh, JFE 2020).
methods.why: Principled way to combine weak signals; same input bottleneck as section 3.

methods.name: Cointegration pairs / stat arb
methods.definition: Trade spreads of co-moving pairs back to mean.
methods.evidence: Up to 11% annual excess 1962-2002 (Gatev, Goetzmann & Rouwenhorst, RFS 2006); simple pairs profits declined sharply in later years (Do & Faff, FAJ 2010).
methods.why: Needs shorting (not in an ISA), high turnover, decayed.

methods.name: PCA / IPCA factor models
methods.definition: Latent factors with loadings driven by characteristics.
methods.evidence: IPCA prices anomalies with few factors on full CRSP (Kelly, Pruitt & Su, JFE 2019).
methods.why: Better as a risk decomposition ("your list is 80% one factor") than a picker.

methods.name: Covariance shrinkage (Ledoit-Wolf) for risk
methods.definition: Stable covariance matrix for portfolio risk and diversification checks.
methods.evidence: Shrinkage estimator dominates the sample covariance when stocks outnumber observations (Ledoit & Wolf, JMVA 2004).
methods.why: Reliable, cheap; gives honest "how concentrated is my risk" numbers for any satellite list. Little use for a pure index holder.

methods.name: GARCH-style or regime-based market timing
methods.definition: Cut equity when forecast vol is high.
methods.evidence: Vol-managed portfolios belong to the quant archive; cross-ref only.
methods.why: Covered by the trend-overlay pre-registration; avoid testing two overlays at once.

methods.name: Formulaic alphas (Kakushadze 101)
methods.definition: Library of 101 short-horizon price/volume formulas.
methods.evidence: Real formulas used in production; average holding 0.6-6.4 days, low pairwise correlation (Kakushadze, arXiv 1601.00991).
methods.why: Days-long holding periods; costs and retail execution eat them; 5-day IC detection floor (0.013) is above most.

methods.name: Genetic programming / symbolic regression
methods.definition: Evolve trading formulas.
methods.evidence: GA-found technical rules did not earn excess returns after costs on the S&P index (Allen & Karjalainen, JFE 1999).
methods.why: A search engine for overfit; multiple-testing burden kills the confirm test.

methods.name: RL-guided alpha search (AlphaGen and successors)
methods.definition: RL generates formula sets that improve a combination model.
methods.evidence: Gains reported on Chinese A-share indices (Yu et al., KDD 2023, arXiv 2306.12964).
methods.why: Same overfit risk at scale; A-share retail-driven market, not S&P 500.

methods.name: LLM-guided alpha mining (Alpha-GPT style)
methods.definition: LLM proposes factor formulas, harness tests them.
methods.evidence: Human-AI interactive mining framework (Alpha-GPT, arXiv 2308.00016); LLM priors become hidden factor exposures (arXiv 2605.16895).
methods.why: The LLM proposes ideas it read in papers about pre-cutoff data; each one tested burns confirm-set credibility.

methods.name: Deep RL portfolio agents (FinRL etc.)
methods.definition: PPO/DDPG agents allocate across stocks.
methods.evidence: Library and benchmark reports on short windows of large-cap sets (FinRL, arXiv 2011.09607); no independent long OOS evidence of beating buy-and-hold after costs found.
methods.why: RL needs a stationary simulator; returns are non-stationary and the reward is mostly noise. Highest overfit risk per line of code.

methods.name: RL for execution/rebalancing timing
methods.definition: Learn when to place orders.
methods.evidence: Execution RL matters for institutional size, not a few hundred pounds.
methods.why: Order sizes are too small for market impact to exist.

methods.name: Text-based peers (Hoberg-Phillips TNIC)
methods.definition: Peer groups from 10-K product descriptions, refreshed yearly.
methods.evidence: Free data library with text-network industries (Hoberg & Phillips data); used for text-based industry momentum (Hoberg & Phillips, JFQA 2018).
methods.why: Ready-made, dated peer graph to strengthen the relationship graph and discovery; peer momentum is a modest, testable add.

methods.name: Clustering returns for peers or regimes
methods.definition: Cluster stocks by return correlation or days by market state.
methods.evidence: Descriptive tool; no direct alpha evidence.
methods.why: Helps diversification views (do my picks all move together?), weak for returns.

methods.name: Anomaly detection on data feeds (isolation forest + rules)
methods.definition: Flag impossible prices, split/dividend errors, ticker remaps, stale quotes, outlier fundamentals.
methods.evidence: Isolation forest method (Liu, Ting & Zhou, ICDM 2008); own history: junk-fund tickers crashed testbed build, 27 renames, dividends missing from b&h lines (+57.6% vs +71.9%).
methods.why: Bad data has already distorted results here; catching it raises the trustworthiness of every test and ledger.

methods.name: Event anomaly detection (unusual volume/return days)
methods.definition: Flag abnormal days on holdings and trigger the reader.
methods.evidence: Generic; used as a trigger, not a signal.
methods.why: Focuses reading compute on days that matter; supports A-95.

methods.name: Causal factor investing / uplift
methods.definition: Require a causal graph and mechanism before accepting a factor.
methods.evidence: Argument that associational factor research is prone to false discoveries (López de Prado, Causal Factor Investing, SSRN 4205613); no credible uplift-modelling evidence for stock selection found.
methods.why: Useful as a "state the mechanism" box in pre-registration; no tradeable method.

methods.name: Double ML for event effects
methods.definition: Debiased ML to estimate an event's effect controlling for many covariates.
methods.evidence: No finance-return evidence found that beats standard event studies.
methods.why: Event studies already failed for lack of effect, not lack of controls.

methods.name: Google Trends attention (SVI)
methods.definition: Search volume spikes for tickers.
methods.evidence: Russell 3000, 2004-2008: SVI rise predicts +30 bp over two weeks, then almost fully reverses within a year; retail attention (Da, Engelberg & Gao, JF 2011).
methods.why: Small-cap retail effect, short and reversing; Trends data is noisy and hard to get in bulk.

methods.name: Wikipedia page views
methods.definition: Daily views of company/finance pages.
methods.evidence: DJIA pages 2007-2012: view changes preceded moves; trading-strategy profits claimed on 30 stocks (Moat et al., Sci. Rep. 2013); free API from 2015 (Wikimedia pageviews).
methods.why: Free, clean, point-in-time, testable 2015+; original evidence is a small, data-mined study. Cheap to add as an attention feature.

methods.name: Reddit / WallStreetBets
methods.definition: Due-diligence posts or mention counts.
methods.evidence: Pre-GME DD buy calls earned ~5% over a quarter; after Jan 2021 the predictive power vanished (Bradley et al., RFS 2024).
methods.why: Effect gone in exactly the period that matters.

methods.name: StockTwits / X
methods.definition: Retail posts aggregated per stock.
methods.evidence: Aggregated tweets predict earnings and announcement returns, stronger in weak information environments (Bartov, Faurel & Mohanram, TAR 2018).
methods.why: Paid, small-cap leaning, crowded.

methods.name: GDELT tone
methods.definition: Article tone and volume per company from GDELT.
methods.evidence: Data from 2015 (GDELT); no strong peer-reviewed firm-level return evidence found.
methods.why: Free history from 2015 is its real value: a dated text archive for A-04/A-24, not the tone score itself.

methods.name: Job postings
methods.definition: Growth in a firm's job ads.
methods.evidence: Posting changes predict future performance and get a two-day positive price reaction (Gutierrez, Lourie, Nekrasov & Shevlin, MS 2020).
methods.why: Reaction is fast and the data is paid.

methods.name: Web traffic and app downloads
methods.definition: Similarweb/Sensor Tower usage metrics.
methods.evidence: Vendor studies only; satellite-style data mainly helps sophisticated short sellers (Katona et al., JFQA 2025).
methods.why: Paid and already priced by funds that buy it.

methods.name: Satellite, shipping, card spend
methods.definition: Parking lots, ship tracking, transaction panels.
methods.evidence: Satellite retail data let sophisticated investors profit around reports 2011-2017, mostly on bad news via shorting (Katona et al., JFQA 2025).
methods.why: Out of budget and shorting.

methods.name: Patents
methods.definition: Patent grants and their market value.
methods.evidence: Patent value measured from grant-day returns predicts growth (Kogan, Papanikolaou, Seru & Stoffman, QJE 2017); data via PatentsView.
methods.why: Predicts growth, not clearly returns; useful for discovery (innovators outside the universe).

methods.name: Government contracts
methods.definition: Federal award flows per firm.
methods.evidence: Free USAspending API; no strong primary return paper found.
methods.why: Weak evidence, entity matching is hard.

methods.name: 13F holdings: best ideas / cloning
methods.definition: Track funds' highest-conviction overweights from quarterly 13F.
methods.evidence: Managers' best ideas beat the market by 2.8-4.5%/yr, 1991-2005; other holdings do not (Cohen, Polk & Silli). 13F arrives up to 45 days after quarter end.
methods.why: Free, slow, no LLM, testable on 2013+ filings; old sample and filing lag are the risks.

methods.name: Congressional trades
methods.definition: Copy STOCK Act disclosures.
methods.evidence: 2012-2020: senator and House buys slightly underperform; consistent with random picking (Belmont et al., J. Public Econ. 2022 / NBER w26975).
methods.why: No edge in the best recent evidence.

methods.name: FINRA short interest
methods.definition: Days-to-cover or short interest ratio per stock; aggregate short interest for the market.
methods.evidence: Aggregate short interest is a strong market predictor: OOS annual R² 13.24% (1973-2013) (Rapach, Ringgenberg & Zhou, JFE 2016); data twice monthly (FINRA). Firm-level shorting anomaly: quant archive.
methods.why: Free, informed-trader data, works on the existing harness; the market-timing version is one series (low power) and post-2013 performance unknown.

methods.name: Options-implied signals (IV smirk, IV spread, put-call)
methods.definition: Cross-section of option-implied skew and call-put IV gaps.
methods.evidence: Steepest-smirk stocks underperform by 10.9%/yr, 1996-2005 (Xing, Zhang & Zhao, JFQA 2010); expensive-call stocks beat expensive-put stocks by 50 bp/week, shrinking over time (Cremers & Weinbaum, JFQA 2010).
methods.why: Credible, large-cap-relevant, but no free history: start a daily logger now, testable in 2-3 years.

methods.name: ETF flows
methods.definition: Creation/redemption flows predicting ETF returns.
methods.evidence: Short high-flow, long low-flow ETFs earns 1.1-2.0%/month (non-fundamental demand reverses) (Brown, Davies & Ringgenberg, RoF 2021).
methods.why: Needs shorting ETFs; not usable in an ISA.

methods.name: SEC comment letters
methods.definition: Staff questions on filings (CORRESP/UPLOAD), released after review.
methods.evidence: Insider selling rises before revenue-recognition comment letters become public; returns drift 1-5% lower over the 50 days after release (Dechow, Lawrence & Ryans, TAR 2016).
methods.why: Information leaks before public release; valuable as a red-flag in holding reports more than a signal.

methods.name: Insider Form 4 text (plans, footnotes)
methods.definition: Separate routine 10b5-1 trades from opportunistic ones using footnotes.
methods.evidence: Insider buys already FAIL here; opportunistic-vs-routine is the quant archive's.
methods.why: Refinement of a failed signal; small chance it rescues it.

methods.name: Behaviour guardrails
methods.definition: Pre-trade checklist and cooling-off: "is this in the plan? did a drop just happen? is this a chase?", plus a log of overrides.
methods.evidence: Most active traders earned 11.4%/yr vs market 17.9% (Barber & Odean, JF 2000); average investor dollar trailed its funds by 1.1%/yr over 10 years from bad timing (Morningstar Mind the Gap 2024).
methods.why: The behaviour gap is larger than any alpha found here and protecting the b&h plan is the highest-value job left.

methods.name: Tax, ISA and fee assistant
methods.definition: Track ISA allowance use, compare fund OCFs and platform fees, flag fee drag and minimum-fee traps on small balances.
methods.evidence: Rules: GOV.UK ISA; after costs the average active pound must trail passive (Sharpe, Arithmetic of Active Management).
methods.why: Fees are a certain, known-size gain; on a small pot a flat platform fee can exceed any factor premium.

methods.name: Data-error catcher with LLM triage
methods.definition: A-76 plus an LLM that explains each flag ("split on 2026-05-12 not applied?") for the user.
methods.evidence: Own failures (junk tickers, renames, missing dividends); isolation forest.
methods.why: Every verdict depends on the data; this raises trust in all of them.

methods.name: Position explainer
methods.definition: For each holding: why it is owned, what changed since purchase, how it moved vs index, in plain English with links.
methods.evidence: LLMs as auditable information interfaces are the recommended safe role (arXiv 2605.16895).
methods.why: Better understanding reduces panic selling; no return claim needed.

methods.name: Filing "what changed" digest for holdings
methods.definition: On each 10-K/10-Q of a held name: new risk factors, changed guidance, new lawsuits (A-08/A-09 machinery, read by an LLM).
methods.evidence: Text changes predict bad news later (Lazy Prices).
methods.why: Saves reading time and surfaces red flags; doubles as the A-08 test pipeline.

methods.name: Risk monitor
methods.definition: Alerts on concentration (A-66), forecast vol spikes (A-60), drawdown vs plan, and flagged events (fraud, delisting, going-concern, comment letters).
methods.evidence: Vol forecasting (Corsi 2009); shrinkage covariance (Ledoit & Wolf 2004).
methods.why: Prevents the rare large single-stock loss; mostly matters for the satellite sleeve.

methods.name: Experiment-hygiene assistant
methods.definition: Checks each new signal: pre-registered? post-cutoff only? power at expected IC? counts tests run so far; refuses to label a result before confirm.
methods.evidence: Leakage and short-window failures in LLM finance (arXiv 2510.07920, arXiv 2605.16895).
methods.why: Cheap, protects against fooling yourself, which is the main risk of an alpha search.
methods.archive_note: Tried-other (pre-registration and harness exist; checks manual)

methods.name: Natural-language queries over own ledgers (local text-to-SQL)
methods.definition: "How did satellite picks do since June vs ACWI?" answered from research.db.
methods.evidence: Convenience; no return claim.
methods.why: Lowers friction to check results honestly; GUI parity needed.

methods.name: Research agent as reading aid, not a signal
methods.definition: Keep the ReAct agent for summaries and source-finding; drop its buy/sell verdict.
methods.evidence: Own: verdict hit rate 56% vs 59.5% base.
methods.why: Keeps the useful part, removes a below-base-rate signal that could tempt trades.

methods.name: Momentum 12-1 (h20)
methods.definition: 12-1 momentum: the past year to the last close, leaving out its last month; cross-sectional IC on sector-excess returns at h20.

methods.name: 1-month reversal (h5)
methods.definition: 1-month reversal: minus the last month's return to the last close; IC at h5.

methods.name: SUE / PEAD from XBRL (h60)
methods.definition: SUE: quarterly EPS minus the same quarter a year before, over the spread of the 8 changes before it; held from the day after its filing; IC at h60.

methods.name: Earnings yield (h20)
methods.definition: Earnings yield: trailing-year diluted EPS over the last close; IC at h20.

methods.name: Gross profitability (h20)
methods.definition: Gross profitability: trailing-year gross profit over total assets at the quarter's end; IC at h20.

methods.name: Insider open-market buys (20/60 d)
methods.definition: Insider buys: distinct officers and directors with an open-market purchase in Form 4s known in the 90 days before; IC at h20 and h60.

methods.name: 8-K 2.02 / 2.01 / insider clusters
methods.definition: Event study: CAR vs sector after 8-K item 2.02 (results), 2.01 (acquisitions) and insider-buy clusters.

methods.name: 8-K 1.01
methods.definition: Event study: CAR vs sector after 8-K item 1.01 (material agreements).

methods.name: Rule strategy, regime lines, regime-v2, learned weights (51 names, 4 y)
methods.definition: Rule-based paper lines on the 51-name watchlist over 4 years: fixed-rule strategy, regime lines (trend, momentum, low-vol blend), regime-v2 and learned weights, each against buy-and-hold.

methods.name: Laya headline classifier
methods.definition: Laya small headline classifier: per-headline sentiment score as a next-day signal.

methods.name: 4B LLM regime tilt
methods.definition: A 4B local LLM reads the news and tilts the regime line's equity weight.

methods.name: ReAct research verdicts
methods.definition: ReAct research agent buy/hold/sell verdicts per company, scored as hit rate against the base rate.

methods.name: 32B reader
methods.definition: 32B local LLM reads post-cutoff headlines (good/bad/unknown per stock) as a next-day signal; job 732 cancelled at 13.8k/154.8k, resumable.

methods.name: XGBoost on the same features
methods.definition: Gradient boosting on the existing few features; skipped because the inputs were weak (see A-35/A-36).

methods.name: Characteristic library (ai-track 04)
methods.definition: About 30 point-in-time characteristics for testbed members from stored XBRL facts and prices, Chen-Zimmermann definitions where possible (value, profitability, accruals, investment, issuance, leverage, momentum family, 52-week high, volatility, beta, MAX, turnover, Amihud, size, dividend yield, SUE, Heston-Sadka), known at acceptance time plus the next-session rule; list frozen before any model run.

methods.name: ML verdict on the characteristic library (ai-track 05)
methods.definition: Ridge and LightGBM on the AT-04 library, target the cross-sectional rank of sector-excess return at h20 and h60; expanding window with yearly refit inside train 2010-2019, frozen for confirm 2020+; compared with the best single characteristic.

methods.name: EDGAR text store (ai-track 06)
methods.definition: 10-K Item 7 and 1A, 10-Q Part I Item 2 and Part II Item 1A, and 8-K 2.02 EX-99.1 text for testbed members 2009 on with acceptance times; infrastructure for AT-07 to AT-09.

methods.name: Lazy Prices signal (ai-track 07)
methods.definition: Cohen-Malloy-Nguyen: per member and section, term-frequency cosine similarity between a filing and the same filing type a year earlier; high similarity = non-changer, signal known at acceptance; IC at h20 and h60.

methods.name: ChronoBERT embeddings (ai-track 08)
methods.definition: Section embeddings from ChronoBERT yearly vintages (filing year Y uses vintage Y-1), 1,024-token chunks mean-pooled; infrastructure for AT-09.

methods.name: AI verdict on ChronoBERT embeddings (ai-track 09)
methods.definition: Ridge from AT-08 section embeddings to sector-excess forward return (h20, h60), yearly refit in train 2010-2019, frozen for confirm 2020+; raw IC and incremental IC after Lazy Prices and the characteristic library; PASS on the incremental result.
